newsitem.title: GERMANY: Political wrangling over ECB top job heats up.
newsitem.headline: Political wrangling over ECB top job heats up.

text.p: Jostling for position at the head of what will be Europe's most powerful monetary institution is intensifying, and analysts see many months of political horse-trading before a final name emerges.

Choosing the first European Central Bank president is a highly-charged step, and the eventual winner will have to prove to Europe and the world that Europe's single currency is sturdy, reliable and well-managed.
"This first Presidency is critical," said John Butler, senior fixed income analyst at WestLB in Duesseldorf.
"If the ECB is going to succeed as an institution that can gurantee price stability and a strong currency, then credibility will have to be established as early as possible."
The current president of the embryonic ECB, the European Monetary Institute's Alexandre Lamfalussy, will in July hand over to Dutchman Wim Duisenberg, head of the Dutch central bank since 1982.
The view among European economists is that Duisenberg will also become the first ECB president early in 1998, but not before a certain amount of jockeying.
"Duisenberg is clearly our preference. The man has a proven track record," said Brian Venables, senior analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.
"His credibility is unquestionable. He has proved at the DNB (Dutch National Bank) that a strong currency and stable price environment are his number one priority."
But Duisenberg has one problem -- he is not French.

France's official position, given at the European Union summit in Dublin in December, is that Duisenberg's appointment as the EMI successor "does not prejudge the presidency of the European Central Bank".

And analysts say there is a strong suspicion in the market that a deal was struck between France and Germany, trading the ECB's headquarters in Frankfurt for a Frenchman in the top job at the start of monetary union.
"I think they did have a deal, and the French are now saying they want that deal to be held to," said Chris Golden, head of fixed income research at Nomura in London.
Reports in Germany's Frankfurter Allgemeine newspaper on Tuesday said Paris had proposed Michel Camdessus, the French managing director of the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
The French government refused to confirm the report, saying talk of who would get the job was "not an issue for the moment".
France's central bank president, Jean-Claude Trichet, is another name thrown into the ring in European press reports.

Economists were unanimous in saying there was really no crack of light between the suitability of any of the mooted ECB possibles, but some said the political angle of any appointment had to be taken very seriously.
"The question really, is which countries will be the most important for EMU. And we have a clear answer -- France and Germany," said one senior economist at a German bank in Paris.

He said apparent scepticism about France's intentions as regards the euro -- some have said Paris favours a weaker European currency against the dollar in a bid to boost competiveness and growth, and cut unemployment -- was unfair.

"The French have driven down inflation from 14 percent in the 1970s to 1.1 percent today. They have fought very strongly against inflation," he said, adding: "In my view it would not be illogical to say that if we have the ECB in Frankfurt, then we have a French presidency."
But some say said that what appears to markets to be blatant pressure from the French to install one of their own in Europe's top job, may well turn out to be a bluff.

"France seems to be shooting the whole EMU project in the foot -- and their own ambitions regarding EMU as a result -- by apparently insisting that the first president is a Frenchman," said WestLB's Butler.
"But I think this is basically a bluff, and France will eventually agree to have Duisenberg and then use it get muscle and leverage further down the line."
